column1: The Role of Carbon Pricing in Food Inflation: Evidence from Canadian Provinces

The thesis titled The Role of Carbon Pricing in Food Inflation: Evidence from Canadian Provinces by Jiansong Xu from the Department of Resource Economics and Environmental Sociology at the University of Alberta  completed on May 22  2024  explores the impact of carbon pricing on food prices in Canadian provinces. Carbon pricing  which includes mechanisms like carbon tax and cap-and-trade  is a tool used by governments to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions. However  there is a concern that such policies may lead to increased food prices  thereby affecting food affordability. This study aims to analyze the changes in food prices resulting from carbon pricing  using Canadian provinces as a case study.

The research employs a staggered difference-in-difference (DiD) approach to assess the impact of carbon pricing on food prices  specifically measured by the monthly provincial food Consumer Price Index (CPI). The findings reveal an overall deflationary effect of carbon pricing on food prices  with average reductions in food CPI of 2% and 4% within and beyond two years of implementation  respectively. The study suggests that these deflationary effects are partly due to reduced consumption  with no significant changes observed in farm input costs. The evidence presented in the paper indicates that carbon pricing does not have an inflationary effect on food prices in Canadian provinces  countering the arguments against carbon pricing policies.

The introduction of the thesis highlights the growing adoption of carbon pricing as a strategy for reducing greenhouse gas emissions  with 39 national jurisdictions implementing such measures as of 2023  covering 23% of global emissions. The two main approaches to carbon pricing are the carbon tax  which is levied on the production or consumption of pollution  and the emission trade system (ETS)  also known as cap-and-trade  which involves the allocation and trading of emission permits. Despite concerns about the impact of carbon pricing on food prices  previous studies have found little evidence of inflationary effects  with some even reporting deflationary outcomes. This study seeks to fill the gap in the literature by examining the long-term effects of carbon pricing on food prices in Canadian provinces  beyond the commonly studied case of British Columbia.

The thesis outlines the history of carbon pricing in Canada  beginning with the implementation of the first carbon tax and cap-and-trade systems in Quebec and Alberta in 2007. The study focuses on the effects of carbon pricing policies in Canadian provinces  excluding territories due to the complexity of their food markets. The data used in the analysis is sourced from Statistics Canada and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The results indicate a deflationary effect of carbon pricing on food prices  which is more pronounced in the long run. The study attributes this deflationary effect primarily to reduced consumption rather than changes in farm production costs.

The thesis also provides a detailed overview of the carbon pricing systems in Canada  including the Pan-Canadian Framework (PCF) announced in 2016  which aimed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and required all provinces to implement carbon pricing by 2018. The federal government introduced a backstop to ensure compliance with the benchmark  leading to the establishment of carbon pricing systems across all Canadian provinces and territories.

In conclusion  the thesis contributes to the understanding of the economic effects of carbon pricing on food prices  providing evidence that challenges the notion that carbon pricing leads to food inflation. The findings support the continued use of carbon pricing as a tool for greenhouse gas mitigation without adversely affecting food affordability in Canadian provinces.
